# What's new in phyr 1.4.0

phyr 1.4.0 is a major update of `pglmm()`:

* **Large phylogenies.** Models are fitted with the sparse precision matrix of the phylogeny (`sparse = TRUE`, the default when possible), so time and memory grow about linearly with the number of species. A binomial model with 5000 species at 20 sites (80,000 observations) is fitted in about 5 seconds, versus about 11 minutes for `glmmTMB()`, with the same estimates ([benchmarks](https://daijiang.github.io/phyr/articles/benchmarks.html)).
* **Laplace approximation by default.** Binomial and poisson models are fitted with the Laplace approximation instead of PQL, with the same estimates and log-likelihood as `lme4::glmer()` and `glmmTMB()`.
* **More families.** Negative binomial (`"nbinomial"`) for overdispersed counts and `"Gamma"` for positive continuous responses, and `offset()` terms in the formula.
* **Inference.** Profile likelihood confidence intervals of the variances (`confint()`), likelihood ratio tests of nested models (`anova()`), and a full profile likelihood ratio test of each random term (`pglmm_profile_LRT()`).
* **Standard model methods.** `VarCorr()`, `ranef()` (one estimate per level, as lme4), `fixef()`, `coef()`, `vcov()`, `logLik()`/`AIC()`/`BIC()`, `predict()` with `newdata`, `simulate()` (residual diagnostics with DHARMa), `update()`, and `tidy()`/`glance()` for broom.mixed and `mice::pool()`, e.g. to combine fits with several candidate phylogenies.
* **Bayesian models with large phylogenies.** `bayes = TRUE` also uses the sparse precision matrix, either as a latent field over all nodes of the phylogeny (giving the posterior of ancestral states) or as a phylogenetic flow (giving the posterior of the rate of each branch).

Some defaults and outputs changed (e.g. `ranef()` now returns per-level estimates; the variances are in `VarCorr()`). See the [NEWS](https://daijiang.github.io/phyr/news/index.html) for the breaking changes, and the vignette ["Usage of pglmm()"](https://daijiang.github.io/phyr/articles/pglmm.html) for examples.

# Installation

To install the released version from CRAN:

```{r eval = FALSE}
install.packages("phyr")
```

To install the development version:

```{r eval = FALSE}
options(repos = c(
  phyr = 'https://daijiang.r-universe.dev',
  CRAN = 'https://cloud.r-project.org'))
install.packages('phyr')

# or
remotes::install_github("daijiang/phyr")
```

# Main functions

The phyr package has three groups of functions:

1. community phylogenetic diversity metrics (alpha: `psv`, `psr`, `pse`, etc. and beta: `pcd`), which were included in the `picante` package originally. They were updated with C++ to improve speed.
2. models to estimate correlation between functional traits while accounting for phylogenetic relationships (`cor_phylo`), which was included in the `ape` package originally. It has new syntax, much improved performance (C++), and bootstrapping option.
3. phylogenetic generalized linear mixed models (`pglmm`), which was originally included in the `pez` package. It has a model formula syntax similar to that of `lme4`, maximum likelihood fits with sparse matrices that scale to tens of thousands of species, and a Bayesian model fitting framework based on INLA.
    + Gaussian, binomial, poisson, negative binomial (`"nbinomial"`) and Gamma families; binomial and poisson models are fitted with the Laplace approximation by default, with the same estimates as `lme4::glmer()` and `glmmTMB()`.
    + Confidence intervals (`confint()`), model comparison (`anova()`, `pglmm_profile_LRT()`), predictions (`predict()`, also for new data), simulations (`simulate()`, e.g. for residual diagnostics with DHARMa), and the methods of the broom packages (`tidy()`, `glance()`).
    + PGLMM for comparative data (`pglmm_compare()`), which was originally from `ape::binaryPGLMM()` but has more features.
    + We hope the model formula proposed here can be used to standardize PGLMMs set up across different tools (e.g. `brms` for Stan).

# Usage examples of `pglmm()`

`pglmm` use similar syntax as `lme4::lmer` to specify random terms: add `__` (two underscores) at the end of grouping variable (e.g. `sp`) to specify both phylogenetic and non-phylogenetic random terms; use `(1|sp__@site)` to specify nested term (i.e. species phylogenetic matrix `V_sp` nested within the diagonal of site matrix `I_site`) to test phylogenetic overdispersion or underdispersion. This should be the most commonly used one and is equal to `kronecker(I_site, V_sp)`.

We can also use a second phylogeny for bipartite questions. For example, `(1|parasite@host__)` will be converted to `kronecker(V_host, I_parasite)`; `(1|parasite__@host__)` will be converted to `kronecker(V_host, V_parasite)`.

For details about model formula, see documentation `?phyr::pglmm` and the vignette "Usage of pglmm()". More application examples can be found in [Ives 2018 Chapter 4](https://leanpub.com/correlateddata).

```{r message=FALSE}
library(phyr)
```

```{r}
# community data: abundance of each species at each site, with environmental
# variables of the sites
dat <- data.frame(
  site = rep(rownames(comm_a), times = ncol(comm_a)),
  sp = rep(colnames(comm_a), each = nrow(comm_a)),
  freq = unlist(comm_a, use.names = FALSE)
)
dat <- merge(dat, envi, by = "site")
dat$pa <- as.numeric(dat$freq > 0)
head(dat)
# the phylogeny of the species in the data
phy <- ape::keep.tip(phylotree, unique(dat$sp))
# phy-LMM
test1 <- pglmm(freq ~ 1 + shade + (1|sp__) + (1|site) + (1|sp__@site),
               data = dat, family = "gaussian", REML = FALSE,
               cov_ranef = list(sp = phy))
test1
# confidence intervals: Wald for the fixed effects, profile likelihood for the variances
confint(test1)
# phy-GLMM (Laplace approximation)
test2 <- pglmm(pa ~ 1 + shade + (1|sp__) + (1|site) + (1|sp__@site),
               data = dat, family = "binomial", REML = FALSE,
               cov_ranef = list(sp = phy))
test2
# is the phylogenetic nested term needed? likelihood ratio test
test2a <- pglmm(pa ~ 1 + shade + (1|sp__) + (1|site),
                data = dat, family = "binomial", REML = FALSE,
                cov_ranef = list(sp = phy))
anova(test2a, test2)
# bipartite
set.seed(42)
tree_site <- ape::rtree(n = length(unique(dat$site)), tip.label = sort(unique(dat$site)))
z_bipartite <- pglmm(freq ~ 1 + shade + (1|sp__) + (1|site__) +
                       (1|sp__@site) + (1|sp@site__) + (1|sp__@site__),
                     data = dat, family = "gaussian", REML = TRUE,
                     cov_ranef = list(sp = phy, site = tree_site))
z_bipartite
```

# Large phylogenies

With phylogenies in `cov_ranef`, `pglmm()` uses the sparse precision matrix of the phylogeny (`sparse = TRUE`, the default when possible), so that time and memory grow about linearly with the number of species. For example, binomial and poisson models with 5000 species at 20 sites (80,000 observations) are fitted by maximum likelihood in about 5 seconds, with the same estimates as `glmmTMB()`, which needs about 11 minutes for these models:

```{r eval = FALSE}
nsp <- 5000
phy <- ape::rcoal(nsp, tip.label = paste0("sp", 1:nsp))
d <- expand.grid(sp = phy$tip.label, site = paste0("s", 1:20))
d$x <- rnorm(nrow(d))
d$y <- rbinom(nrow(d), 1, plogis(0.3 * d$x))
fit <- pglmm(y ~ x + (1 | sp__) + (1 | site), data = d, family = "binomial",
             cov_ranef = list(sp = phy), REML = FALSE)
```
